A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SGShift research. Their readable main text, equations, tables, figures and appendices support a reliable comparison despite substantial revisions.

before.justification: v1 reports original semi-synthetic experiments on three healthcare datasets, sample-size analyses and real-data feature attribution, including Table 2 and Appendices D–E.

after.justification: v2 reports original healthcare experiments plus additional simulations, ACS income analysis, lupus gene-expression analysis and empirical FDR/power results in Appendix E.

M1.justification: The sparse correction framework remains, but v2 changes SGShift-A from pooled loss sums to equally weighted domain-average losses (Equation 4). It introduces e-value/e-BH aggregation for nominal FDR control and a one-pass penalty-calibration option (Appendices E–F). The combined knockoff-and-absorption variant SGShift-KA is removed.

E1.justification: The original three healthcare datasets remain. v2 adds cross-state ACS income prediction and lupus prediction from European and Asian B-cell expression data. It also evaluates previously absent dense, correlated/noisy, global-calibration and interaction-shift scenarios, substantially expanding domain and scenario coverage.

E2.justification: Diff, WhyShift and adapted SHAP remain the feature-selection baselines. v2 adds IPW-based covariate- and label-shift corrections as evaluated alternatives for performance recovery (Section 4.2 and Figure 3). The evaluated SGShift-KA variant also disappears from comparisons.

E3.justification: The reported recall operating point changes from 10% FPR to 5% FPR. New evaluation designs include 1,000 samples per domain, dimensionality/correlation/SNR sweeps, dense shifts affecting over 60% of features, e-BH FDR/power evaluation and a 90%-performance-loss-recovery criterion. The original healthcare splits and 16 generator/base combinations remain. The changed threshold alone does not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained model-mismatch and sample-size analyses, v2 tests violations of sparsity, dimensionality, correlation and noise sensitivity (Table 1 and Figure 2). Appendices J–K add global-calibration and interaction-basis misspecification tests. Figure 3 tests covariate/label reweighting as alternative explanations, while Appendix E evaluates the revised aggregation procedure's FDR and power.

E5.justification: v1's main results table reports point estimates; v2 Table 1 adds 95% confidence intervals across model configurations. Conversely, v1 explicitly reports 100 replicates and standard-error intervals, whereas v2's corresponding captions describe configuration-level confidence intervals without a replicate count. Both retain fixed-seed statements; an actual reduction in runs is not established.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial dense/complex-shift, ACS, lupus and empirical FDR/power results. Sparse-table entries also change: mismatched Diabetes SGShift-K AUC changes from 0.84 to 0.86, and mismatched COVID-19 SGShift-A from 0.87 to 0.80 (v1 Table 2; v2 Table 1). These are revised reported results under changed method/protocol descriptions, not established same-setting gains or losses. v1's per-configuration AUC/recall tables and detailed COVID feature rankings are removed.

T1.justification: v2 substantially revises the estimation argument using averaged loss, local cone-restricted RSC and a derived Lasso cone condition. It adds an SGShift-A estimation theorem and proof sketch (Theorem 3.2; Appendix C). The stability-threshold FDR bound is replaced by an e-BH guarantee under explicit assumptions, and Appendix F adds a heuristic penalty-calibration derivation.

C1.justification: The central sparse feature-attribution contribution remains, but v2's abstract and conclusion claim robustness to complex shifts and violations of sparsity. Its conclusion narrows v1's assertion that true healthcare concept shifts are sparse to the claim that sparse updates often recover predictive performance. The introduction also adds ancestry-dependent lupus prediction as a principal application.

C2.justification: v2 distinguishes sparse predictive corrections from intrinsically sparse data-generating shifts, explicitly limits estimation guarantees versus exact support recovery, and qualifies the shared-misspecification assumption behind absorption. It adds explanations for dense-shift performance, weak-SNR knockoff behavior and background-shift absorption. The genetics interpretation explicitly distinguishes predictive associations from causal biological mechanisms.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies the standardized identity basis, raw-feature grouping, cross-validation versus ranking-based penalty selection, penalty sensitivity ranges and absorption-penalty ratios. The original healthcare preprocessing, sample counts, scikit-learn hyperparameters and code/data availability statements are largely retained in Appendices G–H. These disclosures improve implementation detail without establishing changes to every underlying experiment.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands research positioning beyond v1's statement that WhyShift is the only directly comparable framework. It discusses Singh et al. (2024, 2025) and Subbaswamy et al. (2021), distinguishing their assumptions and objectives. It also grounds revised knockoff aggregation in Ren and Barber (2024) and adds sparse-mechanism and genetics literature.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, problem formulation, method explanation and discussion are extensively rewritten. Related work becomes an introduction subsection, theoretical guarantees are grouped, and experiments and results are integrated. References move before the appendices, whose organization is substantially expanded and revised.

P2.justification: v2 changes the main text from one to two columns and substantially rebuilds the displays. The main benchmark table combines sparse/dense AUCs with confidence intervals; sample-size panels are distributed between main text and appendix, and the dataset table moves to the appendix. New robustness and recovery figures appear, while detailed per-configuration displays and the COVID ranking chart disappear.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important weaknesses by separating stability selection from nominal e-BH FDR control, qualifying the estimation guarantees, and narrowing what real-data sparsity results establish. Tests of dense shifts, interaction misspecification and alternative shift corrections substantially strengthen the evidence beyond v1's predominantly sparse simulations. Removing detailed per-configuration results and explicit 100-replicate reporting reduces auditability, but the improved statistical qualification and testing of assumptions provide a substantial net quality gain.
